title: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
summary: k-means and Lloyd, Gaussian mixtures and EM, choosing k, DBSCAN, linkages and dendrograms, HDBSCAN, embeddings, a million log lines turned into named failure patterns, and evaluation.
outcomes: Run Lloyd's algorithm by hand, compute k-means++ seeding probabilities, and explain why feature scaling changes the answer
Fit a Gaussian mixture with EM, read soft responsibilities, and explain k-means as its hard, equal-variance limit
Choose k with silhouette, VRC, BIC and the gap statistic, and say what each one cannot tell you
Label core, border and noise points for given eps and minPts, and explain why one bridge point can merge two clusters
Build single, complete, average and Ward dendrograms and relate single linkage to minimum spanning trees
Trace HDBSCAN from mutual reachability to the condensed tree, stability, membership strength and GLOSH
Turn a million log lines into weighted, named clusters with templates, TF-IDF, LSA and k-means or HDBSCAN
Score clusterings with silhouette, ARI, NMI and stability, avoiding the dropped-noise and stable-but-wrong traps

blocks.md:
You have ten incidents from last quarter and no labels. Nobody tagged them with a root cause; you only have numbers you computed from each one. The question is whether they fall into a few recurring patterns, and which incidents belong to the same pattern. That is **clustering**: splitting unlabelled data into groups whose members are more like each other than like the rest.

In the prerequisite course you minimised a loss against known targets. Here there are no targets, so every clustering algorithm has to *define* what a good group is, and different definitions give different answers on the same data. k-means defines it with squared distance to a centre. DBSCAN, short for density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise, defines it with density: a group is a region where points are packed closely, and points in sparse regions belong to no group. Neither definition is right in general.

Our ten incidents, two features each. Feature x is how many services logged errors, feature y is how many minutes passed before the first alert fired. Both are small counts of similar size, which matters more than it looks; the end of this lesson changes the unit of y and watches the answer move.

- p1 (1,1), p2 (2,1), p3 (1,2), p4 (2,2)
- p5 (6,1), p6 (7,1), p7 (6,2), p8 (7,3)
- p9 (4,2), p10 (4,6)

Real feature vectors are much longer. Ten points in two dimensions are enough to check every number in this course by hand, and every number below was computed from exactly these coordinates.

blocks.title: Ten unlabelled incidents, x to the right and y upward

scenes.caption: The raw data. Two tight groups of four, one point in the gap between them (p9) and one point far above everything (p10).
What most people say by eye: two clusters, plus two points that do not clearly belong to either. Note that k-means has no way to say that.
The best possible k-means answer for k = 2, found by brute force over all 511 two-way splits (2 to the 9, minus 1): inertia 28.8333. p9 and p10 are pulled into the right cluster.
The best k = 3 answer: inertia 10.8. Now p10 gets its own cluster of one, and p9 still sits with the right group.

blocks.md: k-means takes the number of clusters k as input, and the name says the rest: k groups, each represented by a mean. That mean is a single point per cluster, called its **centroid**, and k-means scores a set of centroids by the total squared distance from every data point to its nearest centroid. scikit-learn calls that total the **inertia**; the clustering literature also calls it the within-cluster sum of squares, the sum of squared errors (SSE) or the potential. "Potential" is the word used by David Arthur and Sergei Vassilvitskii in their 2007 k-means++ paper, which lesson 2 returns to.

blocks.caption: The k-means objective, as stated by Arthur and Vassilvitskii: choose k centres C to minimise the sum over all n points of the squared distance to the closest centre.

blocks.md:
Finding the exact minimum is NP-hard, even for two clusters. The algorithm everyone actually runs is a local search with two steps, usually credited to Stuart Lloyd's 1982 paper on least squares quantisation in PCM. PCM is pulse-code modulation, the standard way to digitise a signal: sample it and round each sample to one of a fixed set of levels. Lloyd asked where to put those levels so the squared rounding error is smallest, which is k-means in one dimension. The two steps:

1. **Assign**: put every point in the cluster of its nearest centroid.
2. **Update**: move every centroid to the mean of the points now assigned to it.

Repeat until the assignments stop changing. Erich Schubert, a clustering researcher whose paper on the elbow criterion we use in lesson 4, notes that because the least squares objective is so natural, this alternating scheme was probably invented several times independently. scikit-learn still calls it by its name: the default of `KMeans` is `algorithm="lloyd"`.

Inertia is the *entire* definition of a good clustering in k-means. Anything you believe about your clusters that inertia does not measure, such as "this point is an outlier" or "this group is a long thin chain", k-means cannot express.

Three consequences follow from the objective alone, before any algorithm runs.

- **Every cluster is convex.** Points go to the nearest centroid, so the clusters are the cells of a Voronoi diagram of the centroids: one region per centroid, holding the points closest to it. A region like that is convex, meaning the straight line between any two of its points never leaves it. The DBSCAN paper makes exactly this complaint about partitioning methods: "the shape of all clusters found by a partitioning algorithm is convex which is very restrictive".

- **Clusters are assumed to be round and equally spread.** The scikit-learn user guide says k-means "clusters data by trying to separate samples in n groups of equal variance" and that "inertia makes the assumption that clusters are convex and isotropic", so it "responds poorly to elongated clusters, or manifolds with irregular shapes". Isotropic means equally spread in every direction, like a round blob rather than a cigar. A manifold here is a curved shape the data lies along, such as a ring or a spiral.
- **There is no noise label.** Every point, however weird, is assigned to some cluster and drags that centroid toward itself.

Schubert explains the round-cluster bias precisely. A Gaussian mixture models the data as drawn from k bell-shaped (normal) distributions, each with its own centre and its own width and shape, and gives every point a probability of belonging to each one, a soft assignment. k-means is the limit case of a Gaussian mixture in which all clusters have an identical, spherical shape and assignments are hard: each point belongs fully to exactly one cluster. That identical shape is "simply a consequence of the sum of squared errors not including any weights depending on the cluster or axis". There is no per-cluster width in the formula, so there is nothing to make one cluster wide and another narrow. Lesson 3 builds that mixture and takes the limit step by step.

blocks.prompt: Compare two splits of our ten points. Split D is the one a density method will produce later: {p1 ... p9} together and {p10} alone. Split K is {p1,p2,p3,p4} and {p5 ... p10}. Which has the lower inertia, and by how much?
blocks.reveal:
**Split K, by almost a factor of two.** Computed from the coordinates:

- Split D: centroids (4, 1.6667) and (4, 6). Inertia **56.0**.
- Split K: centroids (1.5, 1.5) and (5.6667, 2.5). Inertia **28.8333**.

So inertia does not merely fail to find the density answer, it actively prefers cutting the nine-point elongated group in half over keeping it whole and isolating the far point. If what you want is "one group plus one outlier", you are asking k-means for something its objective scores as bad.

blocks.prompt: Keep the same ten incidents, but record y, the time to the first alert, in seconds instead of minutes: every y is multiplied by 60, so p1 becomes (1, 60) and p10 becomes (4, 360). Nothing about the incidents changed. What is the best k = 2 split now?
blocks.reveal:
**{p1 ... p9} against {p10} alone, inertia 14452** (brute force over all 511 splits, in seconds squared).

In seconds, p9 and p10 are 240 apart, while p1 and p5, which sit in different groups, are only 5 apart. Every distance is now almost entirely y, so k-means sees one long cloud of nine low points and one high point, and cutting off p10 is by far the cheapest split. Feature x, the number of services, has effectively been deleted. The best k = 3 split, {p1, p2, p5, p6}, {p3, p4, p7, p8, p9} and {p10}, even slices the data into horizontal bands.

blocks.md:
The prerequisite course standardised features to make gradient descent converge faster. Here the same step decides *what the answer is*. A standard scaler subtracts each feature's mean and divides by its standard deviation, $z = (x - u)/s$; scikit-learn's `StandardScaler` uses the biased standard deviation, `numpy.std(x, ddof=0)`.

With y in seconds, x has mean 4 and standard deviation 2.28, and y has mean 126 s and standard deviation 86.74 s. After scaling, the best k = 2 split is {p1 ... p4} against {p5 ... p10} again (inertia 10.84 in standard units), and the best k = 3 split is the original one with p10 alone. You get the same standardised data whether y was recorded in minutes or in seconds, which is the point: the unit stops mattering.

Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

blocks.question: Your ten incidents really contain one broad recurring failure (eight incidents, spread out) and one tight recurring failure (two incidents, close together). You run k-means with k = 2. What is the most likely outcome?
options: k-means recovers the two groups, because inertia rewards keeping similar points together
k-means splits the broad group in two and merges the tight pair into one of the halves, because that lowers the total squared distance
k-means refuses to converge, because the clusters have different variances
k-means puts the tight pair in their own cluster and marks the broad group as noise
blocks.explain: Inertia has no per-cluster width, so a wide cluster contributes a lot of squared distance. Splitting it buys a big reduction, while separating two nearby points buys almost nothing. This is the "equal variance" assumption in the scikit-learn user guide, and the reason k-means tends to split large clusters and absorb small ones. Noise is not an option: k-means has no noise label.

blocks.question: Which statement about the k-means objective is true before any algorithm is chosen?
options: Inertia is normalised, so a value of 0.3 means a good clustering
Inertia can only be computed if you know the true labels
Clusters are Voronoi cells of the centroids, so each one is convex
Inertia increases with k, which is why you stop adding clusters
blocks.explain: Assignment to the nearest centroid is exactly a Voronoi partition, so k-means clusters are convex; non-convex shapes are out of reach whatever the algorithm. Inertia is not normalised (the user guide: "we just know that lower values are better and zero is optimal"), it needs no labels, and it decreases as k grows.

lessons.title: Lloyd's algorithm by hand, and why the seeds decide

blocks.md:
Let us run the two steps on all ten points with k = 2. The seeds are two data points chosen at random, which is what `init="random"` does in scikit-learn: pick k rows of the data. Say the coin picks p1 (1,1) and p2 (2,1), both inside the left group. Ties in the assignment step may be broken any way you like as long as you are consistent; here a tie goes to cluster A.

The figure shows, for each of the ten points, its distance to centre A, its distance to centre B and the cluster it ends up in. Watch the two centres move and the distances change under them.

blocks.title: Lloyd's algorithm, k = 2, seeded with p1 and p2

scenes.caption: Seeds: centre A = p1 = (1,1), centre B = p2 = (2,1). The two distance rows are computed from those centres; nothing is assigned yet.
Assignment 1: each point takes the smaller of its two distances. Only p1 and p3 are closer to A. Inertia with these centres is 123.0.
Update 1: A moves to the mean of {p1,p3} = (1, 1.5), B moves to the mean of the other eight = (4.75, 2.25). Both distance rows change and inertia drops to 49.5.
Assignment 2: p2 and p4 flip to A, because A is now at (1, 1.5) in the middle of the left group. Inertia with the old centres is 35.25.
Update 2: A = (1.5, 1.5), B = (5.6667, 2.5). Inertia 28.8333, which brute force confirms is the global optimum for k = 2 on this data.
Assignment 3 changes nothing, so the algorithm stops after three assignment steps. p9 is 2.55 from A and 1.74 from B: it joins B without being close to it.

blocks.title: Inertia after every step of that run

scenes.caption: After the first assignment, with the seed centres still in place, inertia is 123.0.
Moving each centre to the mean of its own points cuts inertia to 49.5 without moving a single point between clusters.
Re-assigning p2 and p4 to the nearer centre cuts it to 35.25. Only two points changed hands.
The second centre move reaches 28.8333 and the next assignment changes nothing. Both steps decrease inertia, never increase it.

blocks.md: Why does each step only ever decrease inertia? The assignment step is obvious: every point moves to a centre at least as close as its old one. The update step follows from one identity about the mean, which Arthur and Vassilvitskii quote as a standard result.

blocks.tex: \sum_{x \in S} \lVert x - z \rVert^2 - \sum_{x \in S} \lVert x - c(S) \rVert^2 = |S| \cdot \lVert c(S) - z \rVert^2
blocks.caption: For any set S with mean c(S) and any other point z, the squared error around z exceeds the squared error around the mean by |S| times the squared distance between them. So replacing a centre by the mean of its cluster can only help.

blocks.md:
Why the identity holds: write x minus z as (x minus c(S)) plus (c(S) minus z) and expand the square. Summed over S you get the squared error around the mean, plus |S| times the squared distance from c(S) to z, plus a cross term that is twice (c(S) minus z) dotted with the sum of (x minus c(S)). That sum is zero by the definition of the mean. Check it on update 1: for p1 and p3 the error around the old centre (1,1) is 1, around their mean (1, 1.5) it is 0.5, and |S| times the squared shift is 2 times 0.25 = 0.5.

That also explains termination. Inertia never increases, and no assignment can repeat, so with a finite number of possible assignments the loop must stop. In practice it stops quickly: three assignment steps here, and scikit-learn still caps it at `max_iter=300` with a tolerance `tol=1e-4` on the centre movement.

What the proof does *not* give you is the global optimum. A stopping point is only a local one: no single point wants to move and no centre wants to shift.

blocks.prompt: Rerun the same algorithm with seeds p1 (1,1) and p3 (1,2), the two points stacked on the left edge, instead of p1 and p2. Where does it converge?
blocks.reveal:
**To a horizontal split that no one would draw by hand.** The first assignment sends every point with y = 1 to one centre and every point with y greater than 1 to the other, and that is already a fixed point: centres (4, 1) and (4, 2.8333), inertia **64.8333**.

That is 2.25 times the optimal 28.8333, and nothing in the algorithm notices. Both steps worked perfectly; the seeds decided the answer. Inertia is also the only signal you have, which is the one good news here: 64.8333 next to 28.8333 tells you the run was bad, even without a picture.

blocks.md:
This is not an unlucky corner case. There are 45 ways to pick two distinct data points as seeds here (10 times 9, divided by 2 because the order does not matter). Running Lloyd to convergence from each one gives:

- 11 of 45 reach the optimum, 28.8333
- 19 of 45 stop at 30.4 or 30.4167 (p9 joins the left group, and at 30.4167 p10 joins it too)
- 5 of 45 stop at 32.0, 5 at 52.875, 2 at 56.0, 3 at 64.8333

So 34 of 45 random seedings, about 76 percent, end somewhere worse than the optimum, and the worst is 2.25 times worse. With ten points. Arthur and Vassilvitskii note that the ratio of the result to the optimum can be unbounded even with random seeding, and not because of adversarial inputs.

**k-means++** fixes the seeding rather than the loop. Pick the first centre uniformly at random from the data. Then pick each remaining centre at random too, but with probability proportional to the squared distance from that point to the nearest centre already chosen. Write $D(x)$ for that distance; the paper calls this "$D^2$ weighting".

blocks.tex: \Pr[\text{next centre} = x] = \frac{D(x)^2}{\sum_{x' \in X} D(x')^2}, \qquad D(x) = \min_{c \in C} \lVert x - c \rVert
blocks.caption: k-means++ seeding: the chance of picking x is its squared distance D(x) squared to the nearest chosen centre, divided by the sum of those values over all points. Far points are far more likely, but it is still random, so an outlier cannot force the result.

blocks.title: Probability of each point as the second seed, given p1

scenes.caption: Uniform seeding: every point other than p1 has probability 1/9, about 11.1 percent. One third of the time the second seed lands inside the left group, where p1 already is.
D squared weighting, with the sum of squared distances to p1 equal to 175: p2 and p3 drop to 0.57 percent each, p4 to 1.14, while p8 rises to 22.86 and p6 to 20.57.

blocks.md:
Totalled up: the chance that the second seed lands inside the left group with p1 falls from 33.3 percent to **2.3 percent**, and the chance it lands in the right group rises from 44.4 percent to **72.6 percent**. The bad seedings from the previous figure are exactly the ones this makes unlikely.

One honest caveat from the same bars: p10, the far outlier, gets 19.4 percent. D squared weighting is biased toward outliers, which is why it samples rather than always taking the farthest point, and why you still run several seedings and keep the lowest inertia.

The guarantee below uses three symbols. E means the expected value, the average over the random choices of the seeding. phi is the inertia of the seeds, and phi OPT is the lowest inertia any k centres can reach. The guarantee says that on average the seeds alone are within a factor 8(ln k + 2) of the best possible answer; for k = 2 that is about 21.5. The factor grows only with the logarithm of k, which is why the guarantee is written O(log k).

k-means++ is the only step here with a guarantee. Arthur and Vassilvitskii prove $E[\phi] \le 8(\ln k + 2)\,\phi_{OPT}$ after seeding alone, before a single Lloyd iteration; the iterations can then only lower it. In scikit-learn `init="k-means++"` is the default (a greedy variant that tries several candidates per step), and `n_init="auto"` means 1 run with k-means++ but 10 runs with `init="random"`.

blocks.question: You run KMeans twice on the same data with the same k and get inertia 41.2 and 38.7. What should you conclude?
options: The run with 38.7 is the better local optimum of the same objective, and you should keep it
The data has no cluster structure, since the answer is not stable
Inertia is not comparable between runs, so neither number means anything
k is too large, because a correct k always converges to the same inertia
blocks.explain: Different seeds reach different local optima of one fixed objective, and inertia is directly comparable between runs on the same data with the same k. That is why scikit-learn runs the algorithm n_init times and keeps the best inertia. Instability says something about the seeding, not about whether structure exists.

blocks.question: Which seeding rule does k-means++ use for the centres after the first?
options: The point farthest from all chosen centres, deterministically
The point with the highest local density that is not yet a centre
A point sampled with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest chosen centre
A point sampled uniformly from the cluster with the largest current inertia
blocks.explain: D squared weighting samples; it does not take the maximum. Sampling is what keeps a single far outlier from being chosen every time, and it is what the O(log k) proof needs. Always taking the farthest point is a different algorithm (farthest-first traversal) with different failure modes.

lessons.title: Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft k-means with a shape per cluster

blocks.md: k-means gives p9 to the right cluster with no hint of doubt, although p9 is 2.55 from one centre and 1.74 from the other. Ask it about a new incident at (3, 2) and it answers "left cluster" just as firmly, because (3, 2) is 1.58 from the left centre and 2.71 from the right. Often you want a different answer: *59 percent likely to be the left pattern*. A **Gaussian mixture** gives exactly that, and it also lets each cluster have its own width and tilt, the two things lesson 1 said inertia cannot express.

A Gaussian, or normal, distribution in two dimensions is a bell-shaped density with a **mean** (its centre) and a **covariance matrix** $\Sigma$. The diagonal of $\Sigma$ holds the variance along x and along y (the squared spreads); the off-diagonal entry is the covariance, which tilts the bell. Points of equal density form an ellipse.

A mixture of k Gaussians adds k such bells, each scaled by a **weight** $\pi_j$, the share of the data it is expected to produce; the weights are positive and sum to 1. The density of the whole model at a point x is the weighted sum below.

blocks.caption: N(x | mu, Sigma) is the Gaussian density with mean mu and covariance Sigma. ln L, the log-likelihood, is the sum over all points of the log of the density the model gives them. Fitting the mixture means making ln L as large as possible.

blocks.md:
That log-likelihood is the missing definition behind BIC in the next lesson: it is how well a clustering, read as a probability model, explains the data. It is the same idea as the prerequisite course's cross-entropy, which is a negative log-likelihood; here larger ln L is better.

There is no formula for the best parameters, so the standard fit is **expectation-maximisation (EM)**, which alternates two steps exactly like Lloyd. The **E step** computes, for every point i and component j, the **responsibility** $r_{ij}$: the probability that component j produced point i, given the current parameters. The **M step** refits each component as a weighted average, with the responsibilities as the weights.

blocks.caption: E step on the left; M step on the right. The new covariance is the responsibility-weighted average of (x_i minus mu_j)(x_i minus mu_j) transposed, divided by N_j. These are the update equations in Bishop's Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, section 9.2.2.

blocks.title: EM on the ten points: responsibility of component A

scenes.caption: Start: A at p4 (2,2), B at p7 (6,2), both round with variance 1, weights 0.5 each. p9 and p10 are exactly as far from both centres, so each is split 50/50. Log-likelihood -40.42.
After one M step both components stretch upward to cover the half points, A tilting one way and B the other. p9 and p10 each give A 0.43. Log-likelihood -36.42.
Iteration 2: p10 drifts to B (A share 0.25) faster than p9 (0.34). B is already wider than A, so it is the better explanation of far-away points. Log-likelihood -36.28.
Iteration 3: p10 is now 98 percent B, p9 still 27 percent A. A shrinks toward the tight left group. Log-likelihood -35.53.
Iterations 4 to 6: p9's share of A falls 0.22, 0.12, 0.02 as A narrows toward a standard deviation of 0.5. Log-likelihood -33.65, -33.52, -33.29.
Converged after about 8 iterations at log-likelihood -33.03: A is round at (1.5, 1.5) with standard deviation 0.5; B is centred at (5.67, 2.5), wide and tilted. Same split as the k-means optimum.

blocks.title: Negative log-likelihood after every EM iteration

scenes.caption: Minus the log-likelihood, so lower is better, as with a loss. It falls from 40.42 to 36.42 after the first update.
Every later iteration lowers it again: 36.28, 35.53, 33.65, 33.52, 33.29, 33.04, 33.03. Like Lloyd's inertia, it never goes the wrong way.

blocks.md:
That monotone fall is guaranteed: the Stanford CS229 notes by Tengyu Ma and Andrew Ng prove that EM never decreases the log-likelihood, and Bishop's textbook warns that there are generally several local maxima, with no guarantee that EM finds the largest. It is the same contract as Lloyd's algorithm, so the same remedy applies: several starts (`n_init`) and keep the best log-likelihood.

Now the payoff. Under the final model, a new incident at (3, 2) gets responsibility **0.59 for A and 0.41 for B**, a genuinely split answer. And at (3.5, 2), which is closer to A's centre (2.06) than to B's (2.22), the responsibility for A is only **0.013**: B is so wide that its density there is higher. That is a per-cluster width at work, something inertia has no term for.

Now take the limit lesson 1 promised. Fix every covariance to the same $\sigma^2 I$ (round, identical, not re-estimated) and use equal weights. The responsibility then depends only on squared distances: for two components it is a logistic function of $d_B^2 - d_A^2$ divided by $2\sigma^2$. For p9 with the k-means centres (1.5, 1.5) and (5.67, 2.5), $d_A^2 = 6.5$ and $d_B^2 = 3.03$, so r(A) is 0.39 at $\sigma = 2$, 0.15 at $\sigma = 1$ and 0.001 at $\sigma = 0.5$.

blocks.caption: As sigma shrinks to 0 the exponent explodes, so r becomes 1 for the nearer centre and 0 for the other: a hard assignment to the nearest centre, which is Lloyd's assign step. Bishop, section 9.3.2, derives k-means as exactly this limit of EM.

blocks.title: Soft to hard: responsibility for A along the line y = 2

x.label: x position on the line y = 2

scenes.caption: Shared sigma 2: a gentle slope. p9 at x = 4 is 39 percent A. Points far left are almost surely A, far right almost surely B.
Sigma 1: the slope steepens and p9 falls to 15 percent A.
Sigma 0.5: p9 is 0.1 percent A. The curve is nearly a step at the midpoint between the centres, x = 3.58.
Sigma 0.2: a step function. Every point belongs fully to the nearer centre, which is k-means. Drag the slider to see the whole family.

blocks.md: k-means is EM for a Gaussian mixture with one shared, fixed, vanishing round covariance. Free the covariances and you gain soft memberships and per-cluster shapes; you also gain more parameters to estimate, and a new way to fail.

blocks.prompt: Start EM again, this time with component A at (3, 2) and component B at p10 (4, 6), each round with variance 1. It converges to log-likelihood **-21.04**, far above the -33.03 we just got. Is that a better clustering?
blocks.reveal:
**No. It is a degenerate fit the likelihood loves.** B ends up responsible for just p8 and p10, and with two points in two dimensions a full covariance squashes into a flat line through them: its covariance becomes [[2.25, -2.25], [-2.25, 2.25]], with zero width across the line. Zero spread means infinite density at those points, so infinite log-likelihood.

What keeps it at -21.04 is `reg_covar=1e-6`, which scikit-learn adds to the diagonal of every covariance "to assure that the covariance matrices are all positive". Bishop calls this the singularity problem: a component that collapses onto data points sends the likelihood to infinity, so maximum likelihood for mixtures is not well posed.

blocks.caption: p is the number of free parameters and n the number of points. Each extra component must raise ln L by more than half of its extra parameters times ln n to pay for itself; here ln 10 = 2.303.

blocks.title: BIC for spherical mixtures with k = 1 to 4 on the ten points

scenes.caption: Default reg_covar = 1e-6, best of 50 starts: 89.53, 70.18, 58.95, 38.75. BIC keeps falling, because each new component collapses onto a single point (p10, then p9) with variance 1e-6.
reg_covar = 0.1, added to every variance, so no cluster can be narrower than about 0.32 units: 89.54, 85.23, 82.45, 85.35. Now BIC has a minimum at k = 3, the k-means k = 3 split with p10 alone.

blocks.md: BIC's promise is asymptotic: the scikit-learn guide says it recovers the true number of components "only in the asymptotic regime", with much data actually drawn from a Gaussian mixture. On small or lumpy data, single-point components can buy unlimited likelihood. Look at the fitted variances before trusting a BIC curve, and treat `reg_covar` as a statement about the smallest cluster you believe in.

blocks.question: Under a fitted two-component mixture, a point gets responsibilities 0.59 and 0.41. What does that mean?
options: The point is 59 percent of the way from one centre to the other
The fit has not converged yet, since converged EM always gives 0 or 1
The point is an outlier, because neither component reaches 0.9
The model is unsure: given the fitted weights, means and covariances, there is a 59 percent probability it came from the first component
blocks.explain: A responsibility is a posterior probability of membership, computed from the weighted densities of all components. It is not a geometric fraction, converged EM keeps soft values wherever components overlap, and an outlier far from everything can still get a responsibility near 1 for the widest component.

blocks.question: You fit full-covariance mixtures with k = 1 to 6 on 40 points and BIC falls at every k. The k = 6 fit has two components with variances around 1e-6. What is the best next step?
options: Raise reg_covar or use a simpler covariance_type, refit, and check whether BIC still falls once no component can collapse
Accept k = 6, since BIC already pays for the extra parameters
Switch to the elbow method, which is not affected by collapsed components
Lower n_init to 1, so EM cannot find the degenerate optimum
blocks.explain: Variances near the reg_covar floor mean components have collapsed onto single points, where the likelihood is effectively unbounded, so the BIC penalty cannot keep up. A variance floor or fewer parameters removes the singular solutions. Fewer starts only hides them by luck, and the elbow on inertia ignores likelihood altogether.

lessons.title: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits

blocks.md:
k is an input, so you have to pick it. The obvious idea is to run k-means for several k and look at the inertia. Brute force over all partitions of our ten points gives the exact optimum for each k:

- k = 1: SSE 72.9
- k = 2: SSE 28.8333
- k = 3: SSE 10.8
- k = 4: SSE 5.75
- k = 5: SSE 3.3333

It only ever goes down, and that is not a property of this data. Given any solution for k, Schubert points out you can trivially build a better one for k + 1 by making a point with non-zero error into its own centre. So "lowest SSE" always answers k = n.

The **elbow method** therefore looks for the k where the curve stops dropping steeply, on the theory of diminishing returns: before the elbow you are separating real clusters, after it you are cutting real clusters in half.

The figure plots our five SSE values against a baseline. If you slice a one-dimensional uniform interval into k equal pieces, the total variance falls as $1/k$. Schubert's reasoning: an interval of length b has variance b squared over 12; each of the k slices has length b/k and so variance b squared over 12k squared; adding up the k slice variances gives b squared over 12k, one k-th of the original. So Schubert suggests comparing the measured SSE against the naive estimate $\mathrm{SSE}_1 / k$, which here is $72.9/k$. Anything that merely tracks the baseline is not finding structure, it is just quantising.

blocks.title: Inertia against k, with the SSE1/k baseline

scenes.caption: The five exact optima. There is a bend near k = 2 to 3, but no sharp corner: the drop from 2 to 3 is 18.0 and from 3 to 4 is 5.05.

The grey curve is what pure quantisation of structureless data would roughly give. Our points sit below it from k = 2 on, and the biggest step below it comes at k = 3, which is the signal that real groups are being separated.
Ratios SSE_k divided by 72.9/k: 1.000, 0.791, 0.444, 0.316, 0.229. The big gain is at k = 3 and the curve keeps improving after it, so even normalised there is no single obvious answer.

blocks.md: The elbow is not a quantity, it is a shape in a picture. Schubert's objections: the two axes have different meanings, so an "angle" or "slope" has no units; scaling your data by a factor a multiplies SSE by a squared and moves the apparent elbow; and changing the range of k you plot moves it again. The table in the paper shows every published elbow detector failing both on data with many clusters and on uniform noise.

Criteria that compare with a baseline do better. The oldest is the **variance ratio criterion** of Calinski and Harabasz, which divides the variance explained per extra cluster by the variance left per remaining degree of freedom. It is the one scikit-learn exposes as the Calinski-Harabasz score.

In the formula below, SSE1 minus SSEk is the squared error that k centres remove compared with one centre, shared over the k minus 1 extra centres. SSEk is the error left over, shared over n minus k, the number of points minus the number of means fitted. At k = 2: 44.07 divided by 1, over 28.8333 divided by 8, is 44.07 over 3.604, which is 12.23. A high value means the extra centres explain a lot relative to what remains.

blocks.caption: On our ten points: VRC is 12.23 at k = 2, 20.13 at k = 3, 23.36 at k = 4 and 26.09 at k = 5. It keeps rising, so on this tiny data set it would happily take k = 5.

blocks.md: The other standard answer is the **silhouette**, introduced by Rousseeuw in 1987. It scores each point separately. Let $a(i)$ be the mean distance from point i to the other points in its own cluster, and $b(i)$ the mean distance to the points of the nearest other cluster.

blocks.caption: Near 1 means the point is much closer to its own cluster than to the next one; near 0 means it is on the boundary; negative means it is on average closer to another cluster than to its own.

blocks.md:
Worked on the optimal k = 2 split, {p1,p2,p3,p4} and {p5 ... p10}.

For p1: distances to p2, p3, p4 are 1.00, 1.00, 1.41, so $a = 1.1381$. Distances to the six points of the other cluster are 5.00, 6.00, 5.10, 6.32, 3.16, 5.83, so $b = 5.2361$ and $s = 0.7827$.

For p9: it is in the right cluster, so $a$ is its mean distance to p5, p6, p7, p8, p10, which is $(2.236 + 3.162 + 2.000 + 3.162 + 4.000)/5 = 2.9121$. Its mean distance to the left cluster is $(3.162 + 2.236 + 3.000 + 2.000)/4 = 2.5996$. So $s(9) = (2.5996 - 2.9121)/2.9121 = -0.1073$: **negative**, correctly flagging that p9 is in the wrong cluster for its geometry. p10 scores 0.0746, just as unconvincing.

blocks.title: Mean silhouette of the optimal partition, per k

scenes.caption: k = 2 averages 0.5075. The four left points score 0.72 to 0.78, the right group 0.48 to 0.55, and p9 and p10 drag the mean down.
k = 3 averages 0.5438, the best of the four. Pulling p10 out of the big cluster cuts the mean within-cluster distance for the points left in it, so p5, p6 and p7 climb from about 0.5 to about 0.65.
k = 4 drops to 0.3852 and k = 5 to 0.3278: splitting the real groups hurts. Unlike SSE and VRC, silhouette has a maximum you can point at, here k = 3.

blocks.md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

Two names appear in the advice below. **BIC**, the Bayesian information criterion of Gideon Schwarz, you met in lesson 3: minus twice a Gaussian mixture's log-likelihood plus its number of parameters times ln n, computed there on these ten points: with a small floor on the variances the spherical mixture's BIC is lowest at k = 3, and without the floor single-point components make it useless. More clusters always fit better, but each extra one pays the penalty.

The **gap statistic** of Tibshirani, Walther and Hastie clusters several uniform random data sets to get a baseline SSE for each k, measures the gap between the log of that baseline and the log of the real SSE, and picks the k where the gap stops growing, allowing for the noise in the estimate.

Here is the gap statistic on our ten points, following the paper's recipe. $W_k$ is the within-cluster sum of squares, our SSE. Draw B = 200 reference data sets of ten points, uniform over the range of each feature (x from 1 to 7, y from 1 to 6), cluster each one for k = 1 to 5, and average their $\log W_k$. The gap is that average minus the real $\log W_k$; a big positive gap means the data is far more clustered than structureless data of the same extent. The paper's rule picks the smallest k with $\mathrm{Gap}(k) \ge \mathrm{Gap}(k+1) - s_{k+1}$, where $s_k$ is the standard deviation of the reference values times $\sqrt{1 + 1/B}$.

blocks.title: Gap statistic, B = 200 uniform reference sets

scenes.caption: log of the real SSE (from the exact optima) against the average over 200 uniform reference sets. Surprise: at every k the real data has the larger SSE.

So every gap is negative. It is least negative at k = 3 (-0.148), barely ahead of k = 4 (-0.159); with other random reference sets k = 4 sometimes edges ahead. Either way the largest gap is not the rule.
The reference noise s(k) is 0.2 to 0.4, larger than most of the differences between gaps. With ten points the estimate is very uncertain.
The rule at k = 1: is -0.481 at least Gap(2) minus s(2) = -0.404 - 0.313 = -0.717? Yes, so the paper's answer is k = 1: no evidence for clusters.

blocks.md:
Why negative? Uniform points fill their bounding box, while ours sit at its edges: two groups along the bottom and p10 alone at the top, which stretches the box. The paper also offers a reference that is uniform over a box aligned with the data's principal components; it gives the same picture here (gaps -0.41, -0.32, -0.07, -0.08, -0.13) and the same answer, k = 1, as do other random seeds.

It is the only criterion here that actually answers "no clusters" (BIC could too, since it is defined at k = 1, but on these points it scored k = 1 worst), and on ten points it does. That is not a failure. Four incidents in a corner are not much evidence, and the gap statistic is honest about it where the silhouette, which cannot even be computed for k = 1, is not.

Five criteria on the same ten points: the elbow is ambiguous, VRC says k = 5, silhouette says k = 3, BIC with a variance floor says k = 3, and the gap statistic says one cluster. That disagreement is the lesson. Schubert's advice is to use a baseline-aware criterion (VRC, BIC or the gap statistic) rather than an elbow, and to spend your effort on preprocessing, "because garbage in, garbage out".

blocks.question: A colleague plots inertia for k = 2 to 10, sees the steepest bend at k = 4, and says the data has four clusters. What is the strongest objection?
options: Inertia should go up with k, so their plot must be wrong
The elbow depends on the axis scaling and on the range of k plotted, and the same shape appears even for uniform data with no clusters
They should have used inertia divided by n, which would move the elbow to the right
Four clusters cannot be checked without ground truth labels
blocks.explain: Schubert's point: the curve looks the same on well separated blobs, on 25 blobs and on uniform noise, so a bend is not evidence of structure. Rescaling the data multiplies SSE by a squared and moves the apparent elbow, and starting the plot at k = 2 instead of k = 1 changes it again. Inertia does decrease with k, and dividing by n changes nothing about the shape.

blocks.question: A clustering gives point q a silhouette of -0.35. What does that say?
options: q is an outlier that belongs to no cluster
The clustering has too few clusters, since silhouettes cannot be negative otherwise
q is exactly on the boundary between two clusters
q is on average closer to the points of another cluster than to the points of its own
blocks.explain: Negative means b(i) is less than a(i): the mean distance to the nearest other cluster is smaller than the mean distance to its own cluster members. A value near 0, not negative, means a boundary point. The silhouette has no notion of noise, and negative values can appear at any k.

blocks.question: On a new data set the gap statistic is largest at k = 4, but the one-standard-error rule picks k = 2. Which is the paper's estimate, and why the rule?
options: k = 4, because the rule is only a tie-breaker for equal gaps
Neither: the gap statistic can only choose k = 1 or k = 2
k = 2: the rule takes the smallest k whose gap is within one simulation standard error of the next one, so it does not add clusters that the reference noise cannot distinguish
k = 4, because the rule applies only when all gaps are negative
blocks.explain: Tibshirani, Walther and Hastie choose the smallest k with Gap(k) at least Gap(k+1) minus s(k+1), a one-standard-error style rule. The gap estimates are noisy, so a slightly larger gap further out is not evidence for more clusters. On our ten points the same rule picks k = 1.

lessons.title: DBSCAN: core points, border points and noise

blocks.md:
k-means had to swallow p9 and p10, and we saw that its objective actively prefers cutting the elongated group of nine over isolating the far point. **DBSCAN**, published in 1996 by Martin Ester, Hans-Peter Kriegel, Joerg Sander and Xiaowei Xu, starts from a different idea: a cluster is a region where points are packed densely, and "the density within the areas of noise is lower than the density in any of the clusters". The name spells this out: density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise. It takes no k. It takes two parameters, a radius and a count.

The radius is called eps, after the Greek letter epsilon, the usual name for a small distance. The eps-neighbourhood of a point p is every point within distance eps of p, including p itself. The count is minPts: p is a **core point** when its eps-neighbourhood holds at least minPts points.

blocks.tex: N_{\varepsilon}(p) = \{\, q \in D : d(p,q) \le \varepsilon \,\}, \qquad p \ \text{is a core point} \iff |N_{\varepsilon}(p)| \ge \text{minPts}
blocks.caption: The eps-neighbourhood and the core point condition. The neighbourhood contains p itself, so minPts counts the point: the scikit-learn min_samples doc says "This includes the point itself", and the paper's pseudocode marks a point as noise when its own region query returns fewer than MinPts points.

blocks.title: All pairwise distances, and what eps selects

scenes.caption: Euclidean distances between all ten points, rounded to two decimals. DBSCAN never looks at anything else.
Highlighted: the 20 ordered pairs within eps = 1.5. Row p9 and row p10 are empty, so with minPts = 3 neither can be core, and neither sits inside anyone else's neighbourhood.
Row p9 alone. Its two nearest neighbours, p4 and p7, are both at exactly 2.00, one in each group. Everything about this data set hinges on whether eps reaches 2.00.
At eps = 2.0 there are 26 pairs. p9 gains p4 and p7, and p8 gains p6, taking p8 from 2 neighbours to 3. Those three new links change the answer completely.

blocks.title: Neighbourhood size, role and cluster, for four parameter settings

scenes.caption: eps = 1.0, minPts = 3. Counts include the point itself. p8, p9 and p10 are noise, and the right group is a three-point cluster with p5 as its only core point.
eps = 1.5, minPts = 3. p8 is now within 1.41 of the core point p7, so it joins as a border point. Two clean clusters of four, with p9 and p10 as noise. This is the answer we wanted.
eps = 2.0, minPts = 3. p9 now has three neighbours including itself, so it becomes a core point, and a core point in the gap glues the two groups into one cluster of nine.

eps = 2.0, minPts = 4. p9 has 3 neighbours, below 4, so it is only a border point and the two clusters separate again. It is within eps of core points in both, so it joins whichever cluster is found first.

blocks.md:
The last scene is the one wrinkle in DBSCAN's determinism. The paper is explicit: if a border point falls in the neighbourhood of core points from two different clusters, "point p will be assigned to the cluster discovered first", and apart from that rare case the result is independent of the visiting order.

The chain below is the eps = 2.0, minPts = 3 case written out as the paper's definitions: a sequence of directly density-reachable steps, each one standing on a core point, ending at p8, which is only a border point at eps = 1.5 but becomes core once eps reaches 2.0.

blocks.title: Density-reachability at eps = 2.0, minPts = 3

scenes.caption: Start from the core point p1. Every edge drawn here is at most eps = 2.0, so each endpoint is in the other's neighbourhood.
p4 is in p1's neighbourhood and p1 is core, so p4 is directly density-reachable from p1.
p9 is directly density-reachable from p4. This is the step that does not exist at eps = 1.5, where the nearest neighbour of p9 is 2.00 away.
p9 is itself core at eps = 2.0, so the chain continues through it to p7 in the right group. p7 is now density-reachable from p1, which makes them one cluster.
p8 is in p7's neighbourhood and, with p6 now within 2.0, has 3 neighbours of its own at minPts 3, so it is core here too. At eps = 1.5 it was a border point: reachable from p7, reaching nobody.

blocks.prompt: You are happy with eps = 1.5, minPts = 3: two clusters of four and two noise points. An ingestion bug then writes two extra copies of incident p9, both at exactly (4,2), and you rerun with the same parameters. What changes?
blocks.reveal:
**A third cluster appears out of what was noise.** Each of the three copies at (4,2) now has a neighbourhood of 3 (itself and the two others, all at distance 0.00), which meets minPts, so all three are core points and they form a cluster.

They still do not merge the two real groups: p4 and p7 are 2.00 away, beyond eps = 1.5. But raise eps to 2.0 and that same pile in the gap glues everything together.

Density counts cannot tell a repeated event from a dense region, so duplicates are the most common reason a density clustering changes overnight. scikit-learn suggests exactly this fix: remove near-duplicate points and pass their multiplicity as `sample_weight`.

blocks.md: eps is the parameter that decides everything, and it is not scale free. The scikit-learn doc calls it "the most important DBSCAN parameter to choose appropriately for your data set and distance function" and says it "usually cannot be left at the default value": too small and almost everything is labelled -1 (scikit-learn's label for noise), too large and separate clusters merge. A single point, p9, moved us from two clusters to one by a change of 0.5 in eps.

The paper's own heuristic for eps is the **sorted k-dist graph**: for each point take the distance to its k-th nearest neighbour (here k counts neighbours, not clusters), sort those values descending, and look for the first valley, because "all points with a higher k-dist value, left of the threshold, are considered to be noise". The authors fix k = 4 for two-dimensional data, since the graphs for larger k "do not significantly differ from the 4-dist graph".

With minPts = 3, our 3-dist values sorted descending are 4.47 (p10), then 2.24, 2.24, 2.24, 2.00, then 1.41 five times. The drop from 2.24 to 1.41 is the valley, which puts eps somewhere in 1.4 to 2.2, exactly the range in which the answer flips. Ten points is too few for the heuristic to be decisive, and that is worth seeing: it narrows the choice, it does not make it. The paper's k-dist does not count the point itself, so it reaches one neighbour further than lesson 7's core distances, which do (p10: 4.47 here, 4.24 there).

blocks.question: With eps = 1.5 and minPts = 3, point p8 has exactly 2 points within eps (itself and p7). Why is p8 still part of a cluster?
options: Because 2 is at least minPts minus 1, which is the real core condition
Because it is a border point: it is inside the eps-neighbourhood of the core point p7
Because DBSCAN assigns every non-noise point to the nearest cluster centroid
Because minPts is only applied to the first point visited in each cluster
blocks.explain: p8 is not core (2 is less than 3), but it is directly density-reachable from p7, which is core, so it joins p7's cluster as a border point. DBSCAN has no centroids, and the core condition applies to every point.

blocks.question: Which of these can DBSCAN do that k-means cannot, on the same data?
options: Guarantee the globally optimal clustering for its objective
Run without computing any distances
Return a chain-shaped cluster and label a far-away point as belonging to no cluster
Produce exactly the number of clusters you ask for
blocks.explain: Density connectivity can follow an arbitrary shape and leaves points outside every cluster as noise (label -1). k-means clusters are convex Voronoi cells and every point is assigned. The number of clusters is an output of DBSCAN, not an input, and both methods are distance-based.

lessons.title: Agglomerative clustering: linkages and the dendrogram

blocks.md:
A third family needs neither k up front nor a density threshold. Start with every point as its own cluster, then repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one is left. On our ten points that is nine merges. The record of which clusters merged and how far apart they were is a tree called a **dendrogram** (from the Greek for tree): leaves at the bottom, one per point, and each merge drawn at a height equal to the distance at which it happened.

The only real decision is what "closest" means for two clusters that each hold several points. That rule is the **linkage**.

blocks.caption: The SSE added by merging clusters A and B with centroids c_A and c_B. It follows from lesson 2's identity applied to each half around the merged mean. Merging p9 into {p5, p6, p7, p8}: 1 x 4 / 5 x 6.3125 = 5.05.

blocks.title: Cutting each dendrogram at k clusters, four linkages

scenes.caption: k = 5. All four linkages agree: the left four, p5 to p7, and singletons p8, p9, p10. Small, tight merges are uncontroversial.
k = 4. Still unanimous: every linkage adds p8 to the right group before touching p9 or p10, which stay alone.

k = 3, cut by undoing merges as scikit-learn does. Single (only through how it orders the 2.00 tie), complete and average put p9 with the left group; Ward puts it with the right, the k-means k = 3 optimum (SSE 10.8).
k = 2. Now they split three ways. Single and average isolate p10 (SSE 56.0); complete keeps p9 left and pairs p10 with the right group (30.4); Ward gives the k-means optimum, 28.8333.

blocks.title: Merge heights, the dendrogram read bottom to top

scenes.caption: Single linkage: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1.41, 2, 2, 4. Two merges tie at 2.00, so no single height cuts this tree into three clusters.
Complete linkage: the distance between the farthest members, so heights climb fast: up to 5.83 and 6.32 for the last two merges.
Average linkage sits between the two: 1.21 for joining pairs, 2.60 for adding p9 to the left four, 4.96 to add p10 last.
Ward, in scipy's units: each height h has h squared over 2 equal to the SSE the merge adds. The last two merges add 18.03 and 44.07, a clear jump.

blocks.md: Ward on our points is greedy yet lands exactly on the brute-force optima: its k = 2 cut has SSE 28.8333 and its k = 3 cut 10.8, the same values as lesson 1 and lesson 4. Its merge costs also add up to the whole story: the nine increases sum to 72.9, the SSE of one cluster, and the last two, 44.07 and 18.03, are exactly SSE(1) minus SSE(2) and SSE(2) minus SSE(3). Being greedy, Ward is not guaranteed to match k-means in general, but it is a good way to get a k-means-like answer for every k from one tree.

Single linkage has a hidden structure. A **spanning tree** of the points connects all n of them with n minus 1 edges and no cycles; a **minimum spanning tree** (MST) is one with the smallest total edge length. **Kruskal's algorithm** builds it by sorting all pairs by distance and adding each edge unless both ends are already connected. Each accepted edge joins two different groups, at the shortest distance between them, which is precisely a single-linkage merge. So the single-linkage dendrogram is the MST with its edges sorted, and scipy's notes say its `single` method uses "an optimized algorithm based on minimum spanning tree".

blocks.title: Kruskal builds the minimum spanning tree, and single linkage with it

scenes.caption: Kruskal sorts all 45 pairs by distance. The five edges of length 1.00 that join new points: p1-p2, p1-p3, p2-p4 on the left, p5-p6, p5-p7 on the right. p3-p4 is skipped, it would close a cycle. Single linkage: five merges at height 1.
Next shortest useful edge: p7-p8 at 1.41 (p6-p7 and others at 1.41 close cycles). Merge 6, height 1.41. Two groups of four now.
Two edges of exactly 2.00: p4-p9 and p9-p7. Together they chain the left group, p9 and the right group into one cluster of nine, at a single height. This is the DBSCAN eps = 2.0 merge.
Last edge, p9-p10 at 4.00. Nine edges for ten points, total length 14.41, no cycles: the minimum spanning tree. Its sorted edge lengths are the single-linkage dendrogram heights.

blocks.md:
Two consequences. First, **chaining**: single linkage joined the left and right groups through p9 at height 2.00, exactly where DBSCAN merged them at eps = 2.0 in lesson 5. Cutting a single-linkage tree at height h gives the connected groups of points within h of each other, which is DBSCAN with eps = h and minPts = 2, except that DBSCAN calls the leftover singletons noise. Complete linkage resists the chain, because it looks at the farthest pair, not the nearest.

Second, **ties**. Both 2.00 merges happen at the same height, so a cut by height can give two clusters or four, never three. scikit-learn's `n_clusters=3` undoes merges one at a time and still returns three, but which three depends on how it orders tied merges; scipy's `maxclust` looks for a height instead and returns only two (see the output below). scipy's docs warn that with equal distances it "may choose a different minimum than the MATLAB version".

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

X = np.array([[1,1],[2,1],[1,2],[2,2],[6,1],[7,1],[6,2],[7,3],[4,2],[4,6]])
for method in ["single", "complete", "average", "ward"]:
    Z = linkage(X, method)              # 9 merges: [id_a, id_b, height, size]
    print(f"{method:8} heights {np.round(Z[:, 2], 2)}")
    print("         k=3 cut  ", fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion="maxclust"))

Z = linkage(X, "single")
print("single, cut at height 1.5:", fcluster(Z, t=1.5, criterion="distance"))
ward = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, linkage="ward").fit(X)
print("sklearn ward, k=2:        ", ward.labels_)

blocks.caption: Output, scipy 1.18 and scikit-learn 1.9. fcluster's maxclust cuts by height, so for single linkage the tie at 2.00 leaves only 2 clusters when 3 were asked for. The height-1.5 cut is DBSCAN's eps = 1.5 answer with p9 and p10 as singletons.

blocks.md:
Two ways to read a flat clustering off the tree: cut at a **number of clusters** (`n_clusters`, or `fcluster(..., criterion="maxclust")`, which returns at most that many) or at a **height** (`distance_threshold` in scikit-learn, with `n_clusters=None`, or `criterion="distance"`). A height is a statement in the units of your distance, like DBSCAN's eps; a count is a statement about the answer, like k.

The cost is the catch. scipy's notes give $O(n^2)$ time for these four methods and add "All algorithms use $O(n^2)$ memory": a condensed distance matrix for 100000 points is about 5 billion doubles, 40 GB. scikit-learn's way out is a **connectivity matrix** that only allows merges between neighbours, for example from a k-nearest-neighbours graph, which also makes the algorithm faster.

The scikit-learn guide warns that agglomerative clustering has a "rich get richer" behaviour that leads to uneven cluster sizes, with single linkage the worst and Ward the most regular. Its linkage comparison example adds that single linkage "performs poorly in the presence of noise" while Ward is "the most effective method for noisy data".

blocks.prompt: Lesson 10 will reveal the real causes behind our ten incidents: {p1, p2, p3, p4, p9}, {p5, p6, p7, p8} and {p10}. Which of the four linkages, cut into k = 3 clusters by merge order, recovers exactly those three groups?
blocks.reveal:
**Complete and average do; single does in scikit-learn only by tie order (scipy's maxclust above returns two clusters); Ward does not.** All three put p9 with the left group and p10 alone, a perfect match (ARI 1.0 in lesson 10's terms). Ward minimises squared error, so it does what k-means does and gives p9 to the right group.

Do not read this as "single linkage is better". The tie at 2.00 means single linkage's answer at k = 3 is decided by merge order, and on most real data the chaining that saved it here is what ruins it. The point is that different linkages encode different ideas of a cluster, and only the truth can tell you which idea fits your data.

blocks.question: Two dense groups of log embeddings are connected by a thin trail of a few dozen intermediate points. Which linkage is most likely to merge the two groups early, at a small height?
options: Single, because one short link anywhere along the trail is enough to join the groups
Complete, because it uses the farthest pair and so merges large groups first
Ward, because it minimises variance and the trail has low variance
None, because all linkages give the same dendrogram and differ only in where you cut
blocks.explain: Single linkage measures the closest pair, so a chain of short steps joins the groups at the length of the longest step in the chain: the chaining effect, and the same failure DBSCAN had through p9. Complete linkage looks at the farthest pair and keeps resisting, and Ward pays for the large increase in squared error. The dendrograms differ, not just the cut.

blocks.question: Why is Ward linkage described as similar to k-means?
options: It uses k-means++ seeding to choose the first merge
Each merge is the one that adds the least within-cluster sum of squares, which is the k-means objective, optimised greedily from the bottom up
It computes the same Voronoi cells as k-means at every height
It runs Lloyd's algorithm after every merge
blocks.explain: Ward's merge cost is the increase in SSE, the same inertia k-means minimises, so each cut is a greedy attempt at the k-means optimum. Here it found the optimum for k = 2 and k = 3, but greedy merges are never undone, so in general it can do worse than k-means with good seeding.

lessons.title: HDBSCAN: a hierarchy instead of one eps

blocks.md: One global eps assumes every cluster has the same density. Our two groups are not equally dense: counting the point itself as one of three, the third-nearest point is 1.00 away for p1 to p5 but 1.41 for p6 and p7 and 2.00 for p8. That is already enough that eps = 1.0 left p8 outside while eps = 2.0 merged everything. **HDBSCAN**, by Ricardo Campello, Davoud Moulavi and Joerg Sander, removes the choice. The H stands for hierarchical: it runs the density idea at every eps at once and then keeps the clusters that persist. The scikit-learn docs describe it as performing "DBSCAN over varying epsilon values" and integrating the result "to find a clustering that gives the best stability over epsilon".

blocks.caption: Mutual reachability distance, where core_k(x) is the distance from x to its k-th nearest neighbour counting itself. Dense points keep their true distance; sparse points get pushed away from everything by at least their own core distance.

blocks.md:
With k = 3 (`min_samples=3`), the core distances of our points are 1.00 for p1 to p5, 1.41 for p6 and p7, 2.00 for p8 and p9, and 4.24 for p10. Now build the minimum spanning tree (MST) of the mutual reachability distances, with Kruskal's algorithm from lesson 6 or with Prim's, which the hdbscan docs use: grow one tree from any point, always adding the lowest-weight edge to a point not yet in it. The nine weights come out as 1.00, 1.00, 1.00, 1.41, 1.41, 2.00, 2.00, 2.00 and 4.24.

Adding those edges in increasing order is single-linkage clustering, exactly as in lesson 6, only on the transformed distances. Cutting it at a distance recovers the DBSCAN result for that eps, or almost: the scikit-learn `dbscan_clustering` method notes this gives DBSCAN*, "DBSCAN without the border points". So the one tree holds every eps at once. HDBSCAN then converts distance to a density scale, $\lambda = 1/\text{distance}$, and condenses the tree: at each split, a branch with fewer than `min_cluster_size` points is not a new cluster, its points simply fall out of the parent at that lambda.

blocks.title: The MST edges, before and after mutual reachability (min_samples = 3)

scenes.caption: The nine edges of lesson 6's minimum spanning tree with their plain distances. With mutual reachability, these same nine pairs still form a minimum spanning tree; ties at 2.00 and 4.24 allow others, such as p6-p8 or p8-p10.
The larger core distance of each edge's two ends. p6 and p7 have core distance 1.41, p8 and p9 2.00, p10 4.24; everyone else 1.00.
Mutual reachability is the larger of the two. Four edges get longer: p5-p6 and p5-p7 to 1.41, p7-p8 to 2.00, p9-p10 to 4.24. Sparse points are pushed away; dense pairs keep their distance.
Kruskal in order: the three 1.00 edges join the left four; the two 1.41 edges join p5, p6, p7; then three edges tie at 2.00 and bring in p8, p9 and the bridge between the groups, all at lambda 0.5.
Last, p10 joins at 4.24 (lambda 0.236). Because of the tie at 2.00, which of p8 and p9 counts as joining first is an implementation choice, as the next section shows.

blocks.title: Condensed tree, min_cluster_size = 3, min_samples = 3

scenes.caption: At lambda 0 (infinite distance) everything is one cluster. Increasing lambda means raising the density threshold, which breaks pieces off.
The last MST edge has weight 4.24, so at lambda = 1/4.24 = 0.236 p10 separates. One point is fewer than min_cluster_size, so it is not a new cluster: it falls out as noise.

At lambda = 1/2.0 = 0.5 the remaining nine split into a group of five and a group of four. Both are at least min_cluster_size, so this is a real split and two child clusters are born. This tree breaks the 2.00 tie one way; scikit-learn's differs (below).
Stability, the sum of (lambda_p minus lambda_birth) over members: 2.00 on the left, 0.62 on the right. The left cluster survives to lambda 1.0, the right only to 0.707, which is why it scores lower.

blocks.caption: Cluster stability. lambda_p is the density level at which point p drops out of C. A cluster that holds all its members over a wide band of densities scores high; one that shatters immediately scores low.

blocks.md:
The numbers for our ten points, with min_cluster_size = 3:

- Left child {p1,p2,p3,p4,p9}: born at 0.5, p9 drops out immediately at 0.5 and so adds nothing, the other four survive until lambda 1.0. Stability $4 \times 0.5 = 2.00$.
- Right child {p5,p6,p7,p8}: born at 0.5, p8 drops out at 0.5, the other three survive to lambda 0.7071. Stability $3 \times 0.2071 = 0.62$.
- The root, counting p10 leaving at 0.236 and the nine others at the 0.5 split: 4.74.

Extraction walks up the condensed tree, selecting a parent only when its stability beats the sum of its children's. Here the two children sum to 2.62 against the root's 4.74, so the rule alone would take the root, which is precisely why `allow_single_cluster` defaults to False: "by default HDBSCAN will not produce a single cluster". This selection rule is called excess of mass: a cluster's stability estimates how much of the data it holds above the density level at which it was born. With the root excluded, the answer is the two children, with p10 as noise, and p9 the weakest member of the left cluster.

blocks.prompt: Keep min_samples = 3 but raise min_cluster_size from 3 to 4. In the tree drawn above, the two children born at lambda 0.5 have five and four points. What does HDBSCAN return now?
blocks.reveal:
**It depends on how the tie at 2.00 is broken.** In the tree drawn above both children have at least four points, so the split stands and nothing changes: two clusters, p10 noise. The hdbscan library, which records that tree, returns exactly this.

scikit-learn breaks the tie differently (see below): its right-hand branch at lambda 0.5 is {p5, p6, p7}, three points, now fewer than min_cluster_size, so its points simply fall out of the parent. The root never divides, `allow_single_cluster=False` forbids selecting it, and all ten labels are -1.

min_cluster_size = 2 changes nothing in either: inside each group every MST edge has the same weight, so no pair outlives the rest.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN

X = np.array([[1,1],[2,1],[1,2],[2,2],[6,1],[7,1],[6,2],[7,3],[4,2],[4,6]])
h = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=3, min_samples=3, copy=True).fit(X)
print("labels       ", h.labels_)
print("probabilities", h.probabilities_)
for mcs in (2, 4):
    labels = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=mcs, min_samples=3, copy=True).fit(X).labels_
    print(f"min_cluster_size={mcs}:", labels)

blocks.caption: Output, scikit-learn 1.9. Note p8: noise, not a member of the right cluster.

blocks.md:
p8 is caught in the 2.00 tie too: mutual reachability lifted p7-p8 to 2.00, so three merges tie here instead of lesson 6's two. scikit-learn orders the three tied merges so that p8 joins last; read top-down, p8 leaves the root at lambda 0.5 an instant before the split, so it is noise, and the right child is {p5, p6, p7}. Its stability is still $3 \times 0.2071 = 0.62$, because p8 added nothing either way. The separate hdbscan library, run with `min_samples=2` (its core distance does not count the point itself: the code queries min_samples + 1 neighbours, the first being the point), records the tree drawn above and keeps p8 in the right cluster. With exact ties, membership at the boundary is an implementation detail, so never build logic on it.

The second output line is the **membership strength** that scikit-learn calls `probabilities_`: "proportional to the degree that they persist as part of the cluster", 1 for points that last as long as their cluster, 0 for noise. p9 scores 0.5: it left at lambda 0.5, half of the 1.0 its cluster reaches.

For ranking how strange a single log line is, the hdbscan library adds **GLOSH** outlier scores (`outlier_scores_`; scikit-learn's HDBSCAN does not provide them). From the library's source: take $\lambda_{\max}$, the largest lambda at which any point of the cluster a point left from, or of that cluster's descendants, is still present, and score how early the point dropped out relative to it. In the tree above p10 scores $(1 - 0.236)/1 = 0.764$, p9 $(1 - 0.5)/1 = 0.5$, p8 $(0.707 - 0.5)/0.707 = 0.293$ and every other point 0, which is exactly what the library prints. The docs stress that this catches *local* outliers: points unusual relative to their own neighbourhood, even if they are not far from everything.

blocks.caption: lambda_x is the density level at which x leaves cluster C. Near 0: the point lasts as long as the densest part of its cluster. Near 1: it leaves almost immediately, an outlier.

blocks.md: HDBSCAN trades eps for min_cluster_size, which is usually easier to set because it is a statement about how big a group has to be to matter. In scikit-learn, `min_cluster_size` defaults to 5, `min_samples` defaults to min_cluster_size, and the default `cluster_selection_method="eom"` is the excess-of-mass rule above; `"leaf"` instead keeps the finest clusters at the leaves.

blocks.question: Mutual reachability distance replaces d(a,b) by max of the two core distances and d(a,b). What does that buy?
options: It pushes points that live in sparse regions away from everything, so a lone point cannot act as a bridge between two dense groups
It makes the distance matrix sparse, so the MST is cheaper to build
It normalises all distances to the range 0 to 1, which makes lambda well defined
It makes the clustering independent of min_samples
blocks.explain: A point in a sparse region has a large core distance, so every mutual reachability distance involving it is at least that large. On our ten points it changes nothing for p9, whose distances to p4 and p7 already equal its core distance 2.00; the groups stay apart there because HDBSCAN keeps the hierarchy and selects the two children. The transform depends on min_samples through the core distance, and it does not sparsify or normalise anything.

blocks.question: A condensed tree has a cluster X with stability 3.1 whose two children have stabilities 1.2 and 1.4 (and no further splits). With cluster_selection_method="eom", what is selected?
options: The two children, because eom always prefers the finest clusters
Both X and its children, so every point gets two labels
Neither, because a cluster with children is never selected
X, because its stability 3.1 beats the children's total of 2.6
blocks.explain: Excess of mass keeps a parent when its stability exceeds the sum of its selected children's, otherwise it keeps the children. 3.1 is more than 1.2 + 1.4, so X wins and the children are dropped; the selected clusters never overlap. Always taking the finest clusters is the "leaf" method. On our ten points the root wins this comparison too, which is why allow_single_cluster=False matters.

lessons.title: Clustering embeddings of logs and incidents

blocks.md: A very common reason to cluster in practice is text: a million log lines, three months of alert descriptions, a backlog of support tickets. You turn each one into an **embedding**, a fixed-length vector from a model or from TF-IDF, and cluster the vectors. TF-IDF stands for term frequency times inverse document frequency: one entry per word, equal to how often the word appears in this line times the log of the number of lines divided by the number of lines that contain the word, so words that appear everywhere count for little. The grouping then depends on how you measure similarity between them, and that choice is as important as the algorithm.

For text, similarity almost always means **cosine**: the angle between the vectors, which ignores their length. Length usually encodes something you do not want to cluster on, such as how long the message is or how often that template fired. A log template is the fixed text of a log line with its variable parts, such as IDs and numbers, replaced by placeholders, so thousands of lines can share one template.

Dividing a vector by its length, its L2 norm (the square root of the sum of its squared entries), gives a unit vector pointing the same way. That is L2 normalisation, and it removes length from the picture.

blocks.tex: \lVert u - v \rVert^2 = \lVert u \rVert^2 + \lVert v \rVert^2 - 2\, u \cdot v = 2 - 2\cos\theta \quad \text{when} \ \lVert u \rVert = \lVert v \rVert = 1
blocks.caption: Expand the square: the two squared lengths minus twice the dot product. For unit vectors both lengths are 1 and the dot product is cos theta, so the squared distance is 2 minus 2 cos theta, which only grows with the angle. Rank by one and you have ranked by the other.

blocks.title: Distance between unit vectors as a function of angle

scenes.caption: Both curves rise monotonically from 0 at angle 0 to their maximum at 180 degrees, so on normalised vectors Euclidean k-means and cosine similarity agree on every ranking.
At 45 degrees the squared distance is 2 - 2(0.7071) = 0.5858 and the distance is 0.7654. At 90 degrees they are 2 and 1.4142. This holds only after normalisation.

blocks.md:
Here is what skipping the normalisation costs. Five toy vectors stand in for five log templates; two dimensions keep the arithmetic checkable, but a real embedding would have hundreds.

- e1 = (4, 0), length 4.00, angle 0 degrees
- e2 = (1, 0), length 1.00, angle 0 degrees
- e3 = (1, 1), length 1.41, angle 45 degrees
- e4 = (0, 3), length 3.00, angle 90 degrees
- e5 = (0.5, 2), length 2.06, angle 76 degrees

e1 and e2 are the *same* message, one from a chatty service and one from a quiet one. Cosine says they are identical. Raw Euclidean says they are 3.00 apart, further than e2 is from e3 (1.00), a different message.

blocks.title: Cosine, raw Euclidean and unit Euclidean on five vectors

scenes.caption: Cosine similarity. e1 and e2 are a perfect 1.0, e1 and e4 are orthogonal at 0.0, and the nearest pair after e1 and e2 is e4 with e5 at 0.97.
Raw Euclidean distance on the same vectors. Now e1 and e2 are 3.00 apart, the largest value in e2's row apart from e4, and e2's nearest neighbour is e3 at 1.00. Length has taken over.
Euclidean distance after dividing each vector by its length. e1 to e2 is 0.00, e3 to e5 is 0.5339 and e4 to e5 is 0.2444: the same ordering as cosine, because distance is now sqrt(2 - 2 cos).

blocks.md:
Run k-means with k = 2 on these five vectors, exactly optimally, and the normalisation changes the answer:

- raw vectors: {e1} and {e2, e3, e4, e5}, inertia 5.6875. The chatty copy of a message gets a cluster of its own, because it is simply the longest vector.
- unit vectors: {e1, e2} and {e3, e4, e5}, inertia 0.3102. The duplicate message is reunited and the split is now by angle: the two vectors at 0 degrees on one side, the three between 45 and 90 degrees on the other.

The scikit-learn text clustering example is blunt about this: word count vectors "are then normalized to each have l2-norm equal to one (projected to the euclidean unit-sphere) which seems to be important for k-means to work in high dimensional space".

Why length matters to the assignment step: x minus c, squared, expands to x squared, minus 2 times x dot c, plus c squared. The x squared term is the same for every centroid, so drop it, and dividing by minus 2 turns the smallest distance into the largest x dot c minus half of c squared.

blocks.caption: Expanding the assignment step: the length of x cancels, but the lengths of the centroids do not. A mean of unit vectors is shorter than 1, and by different amounts per cluster, which is why spherical k-means renormalises the centroids after each update so that the comparison really is by cosine.

blocks.md: One more tool appears in the next warning. A singular value decomposition (SVD) factors a matrix into directions ordered by how much of the variation in the data each one carries. A truncated SVD keeps only the top few hundred directions and projects every vector onto them. Applied to word-count or TF-IDF vectors it is called latent semantic analysis, because the kept directions tend to group words that appear in similar documents, a hidden (latent) layer of meaning.

Two more traps on embeddings. First, dimensionality: the user guide warns that "in very high-dimensional spaces, Euclidean distances tend to become inflated" and suggests reducing dimension (for text, a truncated SVD, which is latent semantic analysis) before k-means; the example re-normalises after the SVD, "since SVD results are not normalized". Second, duplicates: a thousand copies of one log line form a dense cluster all on their own, so deduplicate templates or carry counts as weights.

A practical recipe for grouping incidents or log templates: extract templates, deduplicate, embed, L2 normalise, reduce dimension if the vectors are sparse, then cluster. Use HDBSCAN when you expect a long tail of one-off messages that should be noise, and k-means when you need a fixed number of buckets, for example one dashboard row per group. Lesson 9 runs this recipe on a million lines.

blocks.question: You cluster L2-normalised sentence embeddings with KMeans using Euclidean distance. A reviewer says you should have used cosine. What is the accurate reply?
options: They are right: Euclidean distance and cosine similarity disagree on normalised vectors
On unit vectors squared Euclidean distance is 2 - 2 cos, so the assignment step ranks candidates identically; the only wrinkle is that updated centroids are no longer unit length
It makes no difference either way, since k-means ignores the metric and only uses means
Cosine cannot be used with k-means at all, because cosine is a similarity and not a distance
blocks.explain: The identity makes the two orderings the same for unit-length points against a fixed centroid. What breaks the exact equivalence is the centroid: a mean of unit vectors has norm below 1, and the assignment compares x dot c minus half the squared norm of c, so centroid norms matter. Spherical k-means renormalises the centroids to remove that difference.

blocks.question: Raw TF-IDF vectors of log lines are clustered with k-means and one cluster contains only the single longest message, while everything else is in one huge cluster. What is the first thing to fix?
options: Increase k until the huge cluster breaks apart
Switch from k-means to DBSCAN with the default eps
L2 normalise the vectors so that message length stops dominating the geometry
Lower n_init to 1 so the run is faster and more stable
blocks.explain: That failure is the e1 case: an unnormalised vector with a large norm sits far from the origin and from everything else, so it earns its own centroid. Normalisation projects everything onto the unit sphere and leaves only direction. Raising k or switching algorithm without fixing the representation keeps the same bad geometry, and DBSCAN's default eps of 0.5 is meaningless for an unknown scale.

lessons.title: End to end: grouping a million log lines into named failure patterns

blocks.md:
Lesson 8 ended with a recipe in a callout. Here it is as code, on a synthetic stream of one million log lines drawn from 13 message types: database timeouts, login failures, full disks, declined payments, and one kernel panic that fires about 8 times in the whole million. Synthetic, so that every number is reproducible; real logs have thousands of types, but the steps are the same.

The key move comes first. A million lines are mostly the same few messages with different numbers in them, so cluster the **templates**, not the lines.

blocks.title: From a million lines to named failure patterns

scenes.caption: Template mining replaces the variable parts of every line (numbers, hex IDs, UUIDs) with placeholders, then deduplicates. A million lines become 13 rows, each with a count.
Vectorise the templates, not the lines: TF-IDF gives 51 word columns, the SVD keeps 8 directions (about 100 for real data), and normalising makes Euclidean k-means rank by cosine.
Cluster twice if you can afford it: k-means with the counts as weights for a fixed set of buckets, HDBSCAN for a noise set of one-off templates.
